title: UNIT 2: PLANTS
notes:
✓ Plants are multicellular organisms with specialized structures and tissues.

→ They generally contain chlorophyll and produce organic food through photosynthesis.

title: 2.1 CHARACTERISTICS OF PLANTS
notes:
✓ Plants have several characteristics that distinguish them from other organisms.

◆ They are multicellular and have organized tissues and organs.
◆ Plant cells have cellulose cell walls.
◆ Most plants contain chlorophyll and are autotrophic, producing organic food by photosynthesis.
◆ They are generally stationary and remain attached to a substrate.
◆ They grow and develop throughout their life.
◆ They respire and carry out other essential life processes.
◆ They reproduce sexually or asexually.
◆ Plants respond to environmental stimuli such as light, water and gravity.

title: 2.2 NON-FLOWERING AND FLOWERING PLANTS
notes:
✓ Plants are broadly grouped into flowering and non-flowering plants.

→ Non-flowering plants do not produce flowers. Important groups include algae, bryophytes, ferns and gymnosperms. They differ in their structures, reproduction and life cycles.

→ Flowering plants (angiosperms) produce flowers and seeds enclosed within fruits. They have well-developed roots, stems and leaves and are the most diverse group of plants.

→ Gymnosperms produce naked seeds, usually on cones, rather than seeds enclosed in fruits.

title: 2.3 STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION OF PLANT PARTS
notes:
✓ The major vegetative organs are roots, stems and leaves. Each has specialized structures and functions.

◆ Root → anchors the plant, absorbs water and minerals, and may store food.
◆ Stem → supports leaves and reproductive structures and transports water, minerals and organic food.
◆ Leaf → main photosynthetic organ; performs gas exchange and transpiration.

✓ The internal tissues include protective, ground and vascular tissues. Vascular tissues are xylem and phloem, which transport materials through the plant.

title: 2.3.1 INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF A LEAF
notes:
✓ A leaf has an outer layer and an inner middle layer.

◆ Outer layer (epidermis) → protects the leaf. The upper epidermis is usually covered by a waxy cuticle that reduces water loss.
◆ Stomata → small pores, usually more numerous on the lower epidermis, allowing gas exchange and regulating water loss.
◆ Middle layer (mesophyll) → contains tissues involved in photosynthesis.
◆ Palisade mesophyll → closely packed cells containing many chloroplasts; major site of photosynthesis.
◆ Spongy mesophyll → loosely arranged cells with air spaces that facilitate gas exchange and also perform photosynthesis.
◆ Vascular bundles → contain xylem and phloem for transport.

title: 2.3.2 INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF A ROOT
notes:
✓ The root contains tissues specialized for absorption, storage and transport.

◆ Root hairs → increase surface area for absorption of water and minerals.
◆ Epidermis → outer protective layer and absorption region.
◆ Cortex → ground tissue involved mainly in storage and movement of materials inward.
◆ Endodermis → controls movement of water and dissolved substances into the vascular region.
◆ Pericycle → gives rise to lateral roots.
◆ Xylem → transports water and minerals.
◆ Phloem → transports organic food.

title: 2.4 REPRODUCTION IN PLANTS
notes:
✓ Plants reproduce sexually and asexually.
→ Sexual reproduction involves male and female gametes and produces genetic variation.

→ Asexual reproduction does not involve fusion of gametes and generally produces offspring genetically similar to the parent.

title: 2.4.1 NON-FLOWERING PLANT REPRODUCTION
notes:
✓ Non-flowering plants reproduce through different structures depending on the group.

◆ Algae → commonly reproduce by fragmentation and other asexual or sexual methods.
◆ Bryophytes → reproduce through spores and have a life cycle involving gametophyte and sporophyte stages.
◆ Ferns → reproduce by spores produced in sporangia; their life cycle alternates between gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
◆ Gymnosperms → reproduce using male and female cones. Pollen is transferred to the ovule, fertilization occurs, and naked seeds develop.

title: 2.4.2 FLOWERING PLANT REPRODUCTION
notes:
✓ The flower is the reproductive structure of flowering plants.

◆ Sepals → protect the developing flower bud.
◆ Petals → attract pollinators and may protect reproductive organs.
◆ Stamen → male reproductive organ consisting of filament and anther. The anther produces pollen grains.
◆ Carpel/Pistil → female reproductive organ consisting of stigma, style and ovary. The ovary contains ovules.

→ After fertilization, the ovule develops into a seed and the ovary generally develops into a fruit.

title: 2.4.3 POLLINATION
notes:
✓ Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma.

◆ Self-pollination → pollen is transferred to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant.
◆ Cross-pollination → pollen is transferred from a flower on one plant to a flower on another plant of the same species.

◆ Common pollinating agents include wind, insects and other animals. Pollination is necessary for fertilization and seed formation in flowering plants.

title: 2.5 SEEDS (MONOCOTS & DICOTS)
notes:
✓ A seed contains an embryo and stored food that support the beginning of plant growth.

→ Dicot seed → has two cotyledons; cotyledons are usually fleshy and store food. Endosperm is generally absent at maturity. The primary root develops into a root system with lateral roots.

→ Monocot seed → has one cotyledon. The cotyledon is thin and the endosperm is large and well developed. The primary root is commonly replaced by adventitious/fibrous roots.

title: 2.6 SEED DISPERSAL AND GERMINATION
notes:
✓ Seed dispersal moves seeds away from the parent plant, reducing competition and helping plants spread to new areas. Seeds may be dispersed by wind, water, animals and other agents.

✓ Germination is the series of processes by which a seed embryo resumes growth and develops into a seedling.

◆ Suitable moisture, oxygen and temperature are essential.
◆ During germination, the radicle develops into the primary root and the plumule develops into the shoot.

title: 2.6.1 EPIGEAL AND HYPOGEAL GERMINATION
notes:
→ Epigeal germination → the hypocotyl elongates and pushes the cotyledons above the soil surface. The cotyledons may temporarily become photosynthetic.

→ Hypogeal germination → the epicotyl elongates while the cotyledons remain below the soil surface.

✓ The position and fate of the cotyledons distinguish the two types.

title: 2.7 PHOTOSYNTHESIS
notes:
✓ Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to manufacture organic food from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. It mainly occurs in chloroplasts containing chlorophyll.

◆ Equation:
6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
             Chlorophyll

✓ Importance: it provides food for plants, forms the basis of food chains, releases oxygen and converts light energy into chemical energy.

title: 2.7.1 CHLOROPLAST AND PHOTOSYNTHETIC PIGMENTS
notes:
✓ Chloroplasts are the main sites of photosynthesis.

◆ Chlorophyll absorbs light energy needed for photosynthesis. Other pigments can also absorb different wavelengths of light and transfer energy for photosynthesis.

→ Chloroplast structure is specialized for the light-dependent and carbon-fixing reactions.

title: 2.7.2 LIGHT AND DARK REACTIONS
notes:
→ Light-dependent reactions occur in the presence of light and involve absorption of light energy, splitting of water, release of oxygen and production of energy-rich compounds.

→ Dark reactions do not directly require light. They use the energy-rich products of the light reactions to incorporate carbon dioxide and form carbohydrates.

title: 2.7.3 TESTING A LEAF FOR STARCH
notes:
✓ The starch test demonstrates that photosynthesis produces stored carbohydrate.

◆ The leaf is boiled in water, then heated in alcohol to remove chlorophyll, washed and treated with iodine solution.
◆ A blue-black colour indicates the presence of starch.

title: 2.8 TRANSPORT IN PLANTS
notes:
✓ Plants transport water, mineral salts and organic food between roots, stems and leaves through vascular tissues.

◆ Xylem → transports water and minerals mainly from roots toward leaves. It consists mainly of elongated, conducting cells and forms continuous conducting vessels.

◆ Phloem → transports organic food from sources, such as photosynthetic leaves, to sinks such as roots, fruits, seeds and growing tissues.
→ This movement is called translocation.

title: 2.8.2 MECHANISM OF TRANSPORT IN PLANTS
notes:
✓ Water enters roots mainly through root hairs by osmosis. It moves through root tissues toward the xylem and is transported upward.

→ Transpiration pull → evaporation of water from leaves creates a pulling force that draws water upward through xylem.

→ Cohesion → attraction between water molecules helps maintain a continuous water column.

→ Adhesion → attraction between water and vessel walls helps resist downward movement.

◆ Minerals → mineral ions enter roots through passive or active transport depending on concentration and energy requirements.

title: 2.8.3 TRANSLOCATION OF ORGANIC MATTER (FOOD)
notes:
✓ Translocation is the transport of organic food through phloem from a source to a sink.

◆ Leaves are common sources because they manufacture food by photosynthesis.
◆ Roots, fruits, seeds and growing tissues may act as sinks because they use or store food.

title: 2.9 RESPONSE IN PLANTS
notes:
✓ Plants respond to environmental stimuli even though they do not have a nervous system.

→ Important plant responses include tropisms, which are directional growth responses to stimuli.

title: 2.9.1 TROPISM AS A GROWTH RESPONSE
notes:
✓ Tropism is a directional growth response to an external stimulus.

◆ Phototropism → response to light.
◆ Hydrotropism → response to water.
◆ Geotropism/Gravitropism → response to gravity.

→ Positive tropism → growth toward the stimulus.
→ Negative tropism → growth away from the stimulus.

✓ Unequal distribution of the growth hormone auxin causes unequal growth on opposite sides of a plant organ, producing bending.

title: AUXIN AND PLANT RESPONSE
notes:
✓ Auxin, particularly indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), is a plant growth hormone involved in cell elongation and directional growth. Its effect depends on concentration and the plant organ.

◆ In shoots, auxin generally promotes cell elongation at suitable concentrations.
◆ In roots, higher auxin concentrations can inhibit elongation.

→ Unequal auxin distribution helps explain bending of shoots and roots in response to environmental stimuli.

title: PHOTOTROPISM
notes:
✓ Phototropism is the growth response of a plant to light.

→ Shoots normally show positive phototropism and bend toward unilateral light.
→ Auxin becomes unevenly distributed, causing greater elongation on the shaded side of the shoot and bending toward the light.

title: HYDROTROPISM
notes:
✓ Hydrotropism is the growth response of roots to water.
→ Roots generally grow toward regions with greater water availability, helping the plant obtain water needed for photosynthesis, nutrient transport and survival.

title: GEOTROPISM
notes:
✓ Geotropism is the growth response of plants to gravity.

→ Roots are positively geotropic and normally grow downward, while shoots are negatively geotropic and grow upward.
→ The direction of growth results from unequal growth caused by the distribution and action of auxin.

title: 2.10 MEDICINAL PLANTS
notes:
◆ Ruta chalepensis (Tena Adam) → abdominal pain.
◆ Zingiber officinale (Ginger) → tonsillitis, abdominal pain and cough.
◆ Hagenia abyssinica (Koso) → tapeworm.
◆ Artemisia abyssinica (Ariti) → unexplained stomach ache/megana.
◆ Nigella sativa (Tikur Azmud) → intestinal parasites.
◆ Ocimum lamiifolium (Damakesse) → headache, general body illness and fever.
◆ Rosmarinus officinalis (Rosemary) → bronchial asthma, prostate disorder and inflammatory disorders.
◆ Cymbopogon citratus (Tej-sar) → stomach complaints.
◆ Allium sativum (Nech Shinkurt) → abdominal pain, toothache and tonsillitis.
◆ Eucalyptus globulus (Nech-Bahir Daba) → common cold and fever with headache.
◆ Cucumis papaya (Duba) → tapeworm.
◆ Trigonella foenum-graecum (Abish) → mixed with garlic to treat asthma and used to treat gastritis.
◆ Ocimum basilicum (Besobila) → abdominal pain.
◆ Lepidium sativum (Feto) → diarrhea.

title: 2.11 RENOWNED ETHIOPIAN BOTANIST
notes:
✓ Professor Sebsebe Demissew is a renowned Ethiopian botanist and professor of Plant Systematics and Biodiversity at Addis Ababa University.

→ He has made major contributions to the study, documentation and conservation of Ethiopian plant diversity.
